title: Wherever he went (Mark 6:53–56)
hookLine: villages lay the sick in the marketplaces just to touch his fringe

cards: The boat lands at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the lake's western shore. The moment Jesus steps out, someone recognizes him. Then it's like watching news spread before phones.
People run through the whole region. Anyone with someone sick at home picks them up, mat and all, and carries them to wherever they've heard he is. Village, town, farm, it doesn't matter.
Today is just four verses long: no big speech, no single story, a snapshot of what it was like.

teach.b: Here's the last verse, in the old King James Bible: "And whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets, and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment: and as many as touched him were made whole."

teach.h: THE SICK LAID IN THE STREETS.
teach.b: The streets here are the marketplaces, the open squares at the heart of every town. Picture the busiest square you know, lined with people on mats, waiting. And what do they ask for?
Not a speech, not even a word. Just to touch the border of his garment. Remember the woman in the crowd, a week ago?
What she did in secret, a whole region now does in the open.

The border, in Greek, is kraspedon, a fringe or tassel. The law of Moses told the people of Israel to wear tassels on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue, to remember God's commandments.

Many Jews still wear them today, called tzitzit. So the fringe they reached for was very likely one of those: Jesus dressed as an observant Jew, and the sick reaching for the reminder of God's commands on his clothes.
With that, the second part of Mark closes.
Seeds, storms and loaves. The sower from a boat. Why parables.
A lamp on a stand. Seed growing secretly. Asleep on a cushion.
Legion. Go home and tell. The hem of his garment.
Talitha koum. The carpenter at home. Travel light.
John's head. Sheep without a shepherd. It is I.
And now, wherever he went. Next, Mark asks the question straight out: who is this?

how: Many Christians bring the needs of others into prayer by name, alone or aloud in church, and many congregations keep prayer lists for the sick of their community.

o: the fringe or tassel on a garment's corner
the belt tied around a traveler's coat
the hood worn over the head in prayer

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the law of Moses told Israel to wear tassels on their garments
with a thread of blue, to remember God's commandments.
the sick asked Jesus for a long teaching
they asked only to touch the border of his garment.
this passage tells one long story
it's only four verses, a snapshot of what happened wherever he went.

games.q: word spreads that Jesus has landed nearby. someone you love is too sick to walk. what do you do?
o: wait until he comes to your village.
carry them on a mat to wherever he is.
send a message asking him to visit.
games.why: people carried their sick on mats to wherever they heard he was, and laid them in the streets to touch his fringe.

practice: Think of the people who carried their sick to the square, then of someone you'd carry if you could: someone ill, worn out, in need of healing of any kind. Picture setting their mat down in the square.
If you pray, you can bring their need to God by name, the way the villages brought theirs; if you don't, hold them in mind, and ask who could help them that you could reach.
